input: Research cord blood banking before the birth

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Cord blood banking research can range from a basic overview of what it is, to deep comparison of specific banks, medical use cases, costs, and legal considerations — the depth and focus completely changes the plan.

Whether this is for a first child, a family with a known genetic condition, or a family with an existing child who might benefit from a sibling donor changes which aspects of banking (private vs. public, likelihood of use) matter most.
How far along the pregnancy is determines how much time is available and how urgent the research needs to be, since most banks require enrollment before the due date.
Private cord blood banking costs $1,500–$3,000 upfront plus annual fees; if budget is a hard constraint, the research should focus on public donation or lower-cost options.

Some people want purely objective, science-based information (e.g., actual odds of clinical use), while others want practical consumer guidance (reviews, bank comparisons) — the tone and source types should match this.
Knowing what 'done' looks like — e.g., a shortlist of banks, a go/no-go decision, or a document to discuss with a doctor — determines when the research is complete.

Whether the user wants to compile findings into a document, a side-by-side comparison table, or just key talking points for a conversation with their OB shapes how the research should be organized and delivered.

gold.taskTitle: Research cord blood banking before the birth
gold.taskDescription: Gather enough information about cord blood banking options to make a confident, informed decision before the baby is born.

questions.title: What specific aspects do you most want to research?
questions.description: Clarify whether the focus is on understanding what cord blood banking is, comparing private vs. public options, evaluating specific banks, or assessing medical use cases — to set the right scope.

questions.title: Is there a family medical history that makes this more urgent?
questions.description: Determine if there is a known genetic condition or an existing child who could benefit from a sibling donor, which would significantly shift the research priorities.

questions.title: How many weeks along is the pregnancy right now?
questions.description: Establish how much time is available before a decision must be made, since most private banks require enrollment several weeks before the due date.

questions.title: Is private banking's cost a deciding factor for you?
questions.description: Understand whether budget is a hard constraint that would rule out private banking upfront, focusing the research instead on public donation or hybrid options.

questions.title: Do you want scientific evidence or practical consumer comparisons?
questions.description: Determine whether the user wants peer-reviewed data on actual clinical use rates, or more practical guidance like bank reviews, accreditation, and pricing comparisons.

questions.title: What does a completed research outcome look like to you?
questions.description: Clarify the end goal — a final banking decision, a shortlist to discuss with an OB, or simply feeling informed — so the research has a clear finish line.

questions.title: How do you want the findings organized when done?
questions.description: Find out if the user wants a written summary, a comparison table of banks, or bullet-point talking points for a doctor's appointment, to shape how the research is structured.
